{{Short description|Concept in algebraic geometry}}
In [[algebraic geometry]], '''local cohomology''' is an algebraic analogue of [[relative homology|relative cohomology]]. [[Alexander Grothendieck]] introduced it in seminars in Harvard in 1961 written up by {{harvtxt|Hartshorne|1967}}, and in 1961–2 at IHES written up as [[SGA2]]  - {{harvtxt|Grothendieck|1968}}, republished as {{harvtxt|Grothendieck|2005}}. Given a function (more generally, a section of a [[quasicoherent sheaf]]) defined on an [[open set|open subset]] of an [[algebraic variety]] (or [[Scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]), local cohomology measures the obstruction to extending that function to a larger [[domain of a function|domain]]. The [[rational function]] <math>1/x</math>, for example, is defined only on the complement of <math>0</math> on the [[Affine space|affine line]] <math>\mathbb{A}^1_K</math> over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>K</math>, and cannot be extended to a function on the entire space. The local cohomology module <math>H^1_{(x)}(K[x])</math> (where <math>K[x]</math> is the [[Affine variety|coordinate ring]] of <math>\mathbb{A}^1_K</math>) detects this in the nonvanishing of a [[Čech cohomology|cohomology class]] <math>[1/x]</math>. In a similar manner, <math>1/xy</math> is defined away from the <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> [[Cartesian coordinate system|axes]] in the [[Affine space|affine plane]], but cannot be extended to either the complement of the <math>x</math>-axis or the complement of the <math>y</math>-axis alone (nor can it be expressed as a sum of such functions); this obstruction corresponds precisely to a nonzero class <math>[1/xy]</math> in the local cohomology module <math>H^2_{(x,y)}(K[x,y])</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Exercise 4.3}}</ref>

Outside of algebraic geometry, local cohomology has found applications in [[commutative algebra]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Eisenbud|2005|loc=Chapter 4, Castelnuovo-Mumford Regularity}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Chapter 17, Hilbert Polynomials}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Chapter 18, Applications to reductions of ideals}}</ref> [[combinatorics]],<ref>{{harvtxt|Huang|2002|loc=Chapter 10, Residue Methods in Combinatorial Analysis}}</ref><ref name="stanley164">{{cite book |title=Combinatorics and commutative algebra|last=Stanley|first=Richard|year=1996 |publisher=Birkhäuser Boston, Inc.|location= Boston, MA |isbn=0-8176-3836-9 |page=164}}</ref><ref>{{harvtxt|Iyengar|Leuschke|Leykin|Miller|Miller|Singh|Walther|2007|loc=Lecture 16, Polyhedral Geometry}}</ref> and certain kinds of [[partial differential equations]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Iyengar|Leuschke|Leykin|Miller|Miller|Singh|Walther|2007|loc=Lecture 24, Holonomic Rank and Hypergeometric Systems}}</ref>

==Definition==
In the most general geometric form of the theory, sections <math>\Gamma_Y</math> are considered of a [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaf]] <math>F</math> of [[abelian group]]s, on a [[topological space]] <math>X</math>, with [[support (mathematics)|support]] in a [[closed subset]] <math>Y</math>, The [[derived functor]]s of <math>\Gamma_Y</math> form '''local cohomology groups'''

:<math>H_Y^i(X,F)</math>

In the theory's algebraic form, the space ''X'' is the [[spectrum of a ring|spectrum]] Spec(''R'') of a [[commutative ring]] ''R'' (assumed to be [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]] throughout this article) and the sheaf ''F'' is the [[quasicoherent sheaf]] associated to an ''R''-[[module (mathematics)|module]] ''M'', denoted by <math>\tilde M</math>. The [[closed subscheme]] ''Y'' is defined by an [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] ''I''. In this situation, the functor Γ<sub>''Y''</sub>(''F'') corresponds to the '''''I''-torsion''' functor, a union of [[annihilator (ring theory)|annihilators]]

:<math>\Gamma_I(M) := \bigcup_{n \ge 0} (0 :_M I^n),</math>

i.e., the elements of ''M'' which are annihilated by some power of ''I''. As a [[derived functor|right derived functor]], the ''i''<sup>th</sup> '''local cohomology module''' with respect to ''I'' is the ''i''<sup>th</sup> [[cohomology|cohomology group]] <math>H^i(\Gamma_I(E^\bullet))</math> of the [[chain complex]] <math>\Gamma_I(E^\bullet)</math> obtained from taking the ''I''-torsion part <math>\Gamma_I(-)</math> of an [[injective resolution]] <math>E^\bullet</math> of the module <math>M</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=1.2.2}}</ref> Because <math>E^\bullet</math> consists of ''R''-modules and ''R''-module [[homomorphism]]s, the local cohomology groups each have the natural structure of an ''R''-module.

The ''I''-torsion part <math>\Gamma_I(M)</math> may alternatively be described as

:<math>\Gamma_I(M) := \varinjlim_{n \in N} \operatorname {Hom}_R(R/I^n, M),</math>

and for this reason, the local cohomology of an ''R''-module ''M'' agrees<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Theorem 1.3.8}}</ref> with a [[direct limit]] of [[Ext functor|''Ext'' modules]],

:<math>H_I^i(M) := \varinjlim_{n \in N} \operatorname {Ext}_R^i(R/I^n, M).</math>

It follows from either of these definitions that <math>H^i_I(M)</math> would be unchanged if <math>I</math> were replaced by another ideal having the same [[Radical of an ideal|radical]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Remark 1.2.3}}</ref> It also follows that local cohomology does not depend on any choice of generators for ''I'', a fact which becomes relevant in the following definition involving the Čech complex.

=== Using Koszul and Čech complexes ===
The [[derived functor]] definition of local cohomology requires an [[injective resolution]] of the module <math>M</math>, which can make it inaccessible for use in explicit computations. The [[Čech cohomology|Čech complex]] is seen as more practical in certain contexts. {{harvtxt|Iyengar|Leuschke|Leykin|Miller|Miller|Singh|Walther|2007}}, for example, state that they "essentially ignore" the "problem of actually producing any one of these [injective] kinds of resolutions for a given module"<ref>{{harvtxt|Iyengar|Leuschke|Leykin|Miller|Miller|Singh|Walther|2007|pp. 67}}</ref> prior to presenting the Čech complex definition of local cohomology, and {{harvtxt|Hartshorne|1977}} describes Čech cohomology as "giv[ing] a practical method for computing cohomology of quasi-coherent sheaves on a scheme."<ref>{{harvtxt|Hartshorne|1977|p=218}}</ref> and as being "well suited for computations."<ref>{{harvtxt|Hartshorne|1977|p=219}}</ref>

The '''Čech complex''' can be defined as a colimit of [[Koszul complex]]es <math>K^\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_m)</math> where <math>f_1,\ldots, f_n</math> generate <math>I</math>. The local cohomology modules can be described<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Theorem 5.2.9}}</ref> as:

:<math>H_I^i(M) \cong \varinjlim_m H^i \left (\operatorname{Hom}_R \left (K^\bullet \left (f_1^m, \dots, f_n^m \right ), M \right ) \right )</math>

Koszul complexes have the property that multiplication by <math>f_i</math> induces a chain complex morphism <math>\cdot f_i : K^\bullet(f_1,\ldots, f_n) \to K^\bullet(f_1,\ldots, f_n)</math> that is homotopic to zero,<ref>{{cite web|title=Lemma 15.28.6 (0663)—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0663|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu|access-date=2020-05-01}}</ref> meaning <math>H^i(K^\bullet(f_1,\ldots, f_n))</math> is annihilated by the <math>f_i</math>. A non-zero map in the colimit of the <math>\operatorname{Hom}</math> sets contains maps from the all but finitely many Koszul complexes, and which are not annihilated by some element in the ideal.

This colimit of Koszul complexes is isomorphic to<ref>{{cite web|title=Lemma 15.28.13 (0913)—The Stacks project|url=https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0913|website=stacks.math.columbia.edu|access-date=2020-05-01}}</ref> the [[Čech cohomology|Čech complex]], denoted <math>\check{C}^\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_n;M)</math>, below. <blockquote><math>0\to M \to \bigoplus_{i_0} M_{f_i} \to \bigoplus_{i_0 < i_1} M_{f_{i_0}f_{i_1}} \to \cdots \to M_{f_1\cdots f_n}\to 0</math> </blockquote>
where the ''i''<sup>th</sup> local cohomology module of <math>M</math> with respect to <math>I=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)</math> is isomorphic to<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Theorem 5.1.19}}</ref> the ''i''<sup>th</sup> [[cohomology|cohomology group]] of the above [[chain complex]],
:<math>H^i_I(M)\cong H^i(\check{C}^\bullet(f_1,\ldots,f_n;M)).</math>

The broader issue of computing local cohomology modules (in [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic zero]]) is discussed in {{harvtxt|Leykin|2002}} and {{harvtxt|Iyengar|Leuschke|Leykin|Miller|Miller|Singh|Walther|2007|loc=Lecture 23}}.

==Basic properties==
Since local cohomology is defined as [[derived functor]], for any short exact sequence of ''R''-modules <math>0\to M_1\to M_2\to M_3\to 0</math>, there is, by definition, a natural [[long exact sequence]] in local cohomology

:<math>\cdots\to H^i_I(M_1)\to H^i_I(M_2)\to H^i_I(M_3)\to H^{i+1}_I(M_1)\to\cdots</math>

There is also a [[long exact sequence]] of [[sheaf cohomology]] linking the ordinary sheaf cohomology of ''X'' and of the [[open set]]  ''U'' = ''X'' \''Y'', with the local cohomology modules. For a [[quasicoherent sheaf]] ''F'' defined on ''X'', this has the form

:<math>\cdots\to H^i_Y(X,F)\to H^i(X,F)\to H^i(U,F)\to H^{i+1}_Y(X,F)\to\cdots</math>

In the setting where ''X'' is an [[affine scheme]] <math>\text{Spec}(R)</math> and ''Y'' is the vanishing set of an [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] ''I'', the cohomology groups <math>H^i(X,F)</math> vanish for <math>i>0</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Hartshorne|1977|loc=Theorem 3.7}}</ref> If <math>F=\tilde{M}</math>, this leads to an exact sequence

:<math>0 \to H_I^0(M) \to M \stackrel {\text{res}} \to H^0(U, \tilde M) \to H^1_I(M) \to 0,</math>

where the middle map is the restriction of sections. The target of this restriction map is also referred to as the [[ideal transform]]. For ''n'' &ge; 1, there are isomorphisms

:<math>H^{n}(U, \tilde M) \stackrel \cong \to H^{n+1}_I(M).</math>

Because of the above isomorphism with [[sheaf cohomology]], local cohomology can be used to express a number of meaningful [[Algebraic topology|topological]] constructions on the scheme <math>X=\operatorname{Spec}(R)</math> in purely algebraic terms. For example, there is a natural analogue in local cohomology of the [[Mayer–Vietoris sequence]] with respect to a pair of open sets ''U'' and ''V'' in ''X'', given by the complements of the closed subschemes corresponding to a pair of ideal ''I'' and ''J'', respectively.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Theorem 3.2.3}}</ref> This sequence has the form

:<math>\cdots H^i_{I+J}(M)\to H^i_I(M)\oplus H^i_J(M)\to H^i_{I\cap J}(M)\to H^{i+1}_{I+J}(M)\to\cdots</math>

for any <math>R</math>-module <math>M</math>.

The vanishing of local cohomology can be used to bound the least number of equations (referred to as the [[arithmetic rank]]) needed to (set theoretically) define the algebraic set <math>V(I)</math> in <math>\operatorname{Spec}(R)</math>. If <math>J</math> has the same radical as <math>I</math>, and is generated by <math>n</math> elements, then the Čech complex on the generators of <math>J</math> has no terms in degree <math>i > n</math>. The least number of generators among all ideals <math>J</math> such that <math>\sqrt{J}=\sqrt{I}</math> is the arithmetic rank of <math>I</math>, denoted <math>\operatorname{ara}(I)</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Definition 3.3.2}}</ref> Since the local cohomology with respect to <math>I</math> may be computed using any such ideal, it follows that <math>H^i_I(M)=0</math> for <math>i>\operatorname{ara}(I)</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Remark 5.1.20}}</ref>

===Graded local cohomology and projective geometry===

When <math>R</math> is [[graded ring|graded]] by <math>\mathbb{N}</math>, <math>I</math> is generated by homogeneous elements, and <math>M</math> is a graded module, there is a natural grading on the local cohomology module <math>H^i_I(M)</math> that is compatible with the gradings of <math>M</math> and <math>R</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Corollary 12.3.3}}</ref> All of the basic properties of local cohomology expressed in this article are compatible with the graded structure.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Chapter 13}}</ref> If <math>M</math> is finitely generated and <math>I=\mathfrak{m}</math> is the ideal generated by the elements of <math>R</math> having positive degree, then the graded components <math>H^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(M)_n</math> are finitely generated over <math>R</math> and vanish for sufficiently large <math>n</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Proposition 15.1.5}}</ref>

The case where <math>I=\mathfrak m</math> is the ideal generated by all elements of positive degree (sometimes called the [[irrelevant ideal]]) is particularly special, due to its relationship with [[projective geometry]].<ref>{{harvtxt|Eisenbud|1995|loc=§A.4}}</ref> In this case, there is an isomorphism

:<math>H^{i+1}_{\mathfrak m}(M)\cong \bigoplus_{k \in \mathbf Z} H^i(\text{Proj}(R), \tilde M(k))</math>

where <math>\text{Proj}(R)</math> is the [[Proj construction|projective scheme]] associated to <math>R</math>, and <math>(k)</math> denotes the [[Serre twist]]. This isomorphism is graded, giving

:<math>H^{i+1}_{\mathfrak m}(M)_n \cong H^i(\text{Proj}(R), \tilde M(n))</math>

in all degrees <math>n</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Theorem 20.4.4}}</ref>

This isomorphism relates local cohomology with the [[Coherent sheaf cohomology|global cohomology of projective schemes]]. For example, the [[Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity]] can be formulated using local cohomology<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Definition 15.2.9}}</ref> as

:<math>\text{reg}(M) = \text{sup}\{\text{end}(H^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(M))+i\,|\, 0\leq i\leq \text{dim}(M)\}</math>

where <math>\text{end}(N)</math> denotes the highest degree <math>t</math> such that <math>N_t\neq 0</math>. Local cohomology can be used to prove certain upper bound results concerning the regularity.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Chapter 16}}</ref>

==Examples==

===Top local cohomology===
Using the Čech complex, if <math>I=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)R</math> the local cohomology module <math>H^n_I(M)</math> is generated over <math>R</math> by the images of the [[Localization (commutative algebra)|formal fractions]]
:<math>\left[\frac{m}{f_1^{t_1}\cdots f_n^{t_n}}\right]</math>
for <math>m\in M</math> and <math>t_1,\ldots,t_n\geq 1</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Iyengar|Leuschke|Leykin|Miller|Miller|Singh|Walther|2007|loc=Corollary 7.14}}</ref> This fraction corresponds to a nonzero element of <math>H^n_I(M)</math> if and only if there is no <math>k\geq 0</math> such that <math>(f_1\cdots f_t)^k m \in (f_1^{t_1+k},\ldots,f_t^{t_n+k})M</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Exercise 5.1.21}}</ref> For example, if <math>t_i=1</math>, then
:<math>f_i\cdot \left[\frac{m}{f_1^{t_1}\cdots f_i\cdots f_n^{t_n}}\right]=0.</math>

* If <math>K</math> is a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] and <math>R=K[x_1,\ldots,x_n]</math> is a [[polynomial ring]] over <math>K</math> in <math>n</math> variables, then the local cohomology module <math>H^n_{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)}(K[x_1,\ldots,x_n])</math> may be regarded as a [[vector space]] over <math>K</math> with basis given by (the [[Čech cohomology]] classes of) the inverse monomials <math>\left[x_1^{-t_1}\cdots x_n^{-t_n}\right]</math> for <math>t_1,\ldots,t_n\geq 1</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Iyengar|Leuschke|Leykin|Miller|Miller|Singh|Walther|2007|loc=Exercise 7.16}}</ref> As an <math>R</math>-module, multiplication by <math>x_i</math> lowers <math>t_i</math> by 1, subject to the condition <math>x_i\cdot \left[x_1^{-t_1}\cdots x_i^{-1}\cdots x_n^{-t_n}\right]=0.</math> Because the powers <math>t_i</math> cannot be increased by multiplying with elements of <math>R</math>, the module <math>H^n_{(x_1,\ldots,x_n)}(K[x_1,\ldots,x_n])</math> is not [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]].

===Examples of H<sup>1</sup>===
If <math>H^0(U,\tilde R)</math> is known (where <math>U=\operatorname{Spec}(R)-V(I)</math>), the module <math>H^1_I(R)</math> can sometimes be computed explicitly using the sequence

:<math>0 \to H_I^0(R) \to R \to H^0(U, \tilde R) \to H^1_I(R) \to 0.</math>

In the following examples, <math>K</math> is any [[Field (mathematics)|field]].

* If <math>R=K[X,Y^2,XY,Y^3]</math> and <math>I=(X,Y^2)R</math>, then <math>H^0(U,\tilde R)=K[X,Y]</math> and as a vector space over <math>K</math>, the first local cohomology module <math>H^1_I(R)</math> is <math>K[X,Y]/K[X,Y^2,XY,Y^3]</math>, a 1-dimensional <math>K</math> vector space generated by <math>Y</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Exercise 2.3.6(v)}}</ref>
* If <math>R=K[X,Y]/(X^2,XY)</math> and <math>\mathfrak{m}=(X,Y)R</math>, then <math>\Gamma_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)=xR</math> and <math>H^0(U,\tilde R)=K[Y,Y^{-1}]</math>, so <math>H^1_{\mathfrak{m}}(R)=K[Y,Y^{-1}]/K[Y]</math> is an infinite-dimensional <math>K</math> vector space with basis <math>Y^{-1},Y^{-2},Y^{-3},\ldots</math><ref>{{harvtxt|Eisenbud|2005|loc=Example A1.10}}</ref>

==Relation to invariants of modules==
The dimension dim<sub>''R''</sub>(M) of a module (defined as the [[Krull dimension]] of its support) provides an upper bound for local cohomology modules:<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Theorem 6.1.2}}</ref>

:<math>H_I^n(M) = 0 \text{ for all }n>\dim_R(M).</math>

If ''R'' is [[local ring|local]] and ''M'' [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]], then this bound is sharp, i.e., <math>H^n_\mathfrak{m}(M) \ne 0</math>.

The [[depth of a module|depth]] (defined as the maximal length of a [[regular sequence|regular ''M''-sequence]]; also referred to as the grade of ''M'') provides a sharp lower bound, i.e., it is the smallest integer ''n'' such that<ref>{{harvtxt|Hartshorne|1967|loc=Theorem 3.8}}, {{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Theorem 6.2.7}}, ''M'' is finitely generated, ''IM'' &ne; ''M''</ref>

:<math>H^n_I(M) \ne 0.</math>

These two bounds together yield a characterisation of [[Cohen–Macaulay module]]s over local rings: they are precisely those modules where <math>H^n_\mathfrak{m}(M)</math> vanishes for all but one ''n''.

==Local duality==
The [[local duality theorem]] is a local analogue of [[Serre duality]]. For a [[Cohen-Macaulay]] [[local ring]] <math>R</math> of dimension <math>d</math> that is a homomorphic image of a [[Gorenstein ring|Gorenstein local ring]]<ref>{{harvtxt|Bruns|Herzog|1998|loc=Theorem 3.3.6}}</ref> (for example, if <math>R</math> is [[completion of a ring|complete]]<ref>{{harvtxt|Bruns|Herzog|1998|loc=Corollary 3.3.8}}</ref>), it states that the natural pairing

:<math>H^n_\mathfrak m(M) \times \operatorname{Ext}_R^{d-n}(M, \omega_R) \to H^d_\mathfrak m(\omega_R)</math>

is a [[perfect pairing]], where <math>\omega_R</math> is a [[dualizing module]] for <math>R</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Hartshorne|1967|loc=Theorem 6.7}}</ref> In terms of the [[Matlis duality|Matlis duality functor]] <math>D(-)</math>, the local duality theorem may be expressed as the following isomorphism.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=Theorem 11.2.8}}</ref>

:<math>H^n_\mathfrak m(M) \cong D(\operatorname{Ext}_R^{d-n}(M,\omega_R))</math>

The statement is simpler when <math>\omega_R \cong R</math>, which is equivalent<ref>{{harvtxt|Bruns|Herzog|1998|loc=Theorem 3.3.7}}</ref> to the hypothesis that <math>R</math> is [[Gorenstein ring|Gorenstein]]. This is the case, for example, if <math>R</math> is [[regular ring|regular]].

==Applications==
The initial applications were to analogues of the [[Lefschetz hyperplane theorem]]s. In general such theorems state that homology or cohomology is supported on a [[hyperplane section]] of an [[algebraic variety]], except for some 'loss' that can be controlled. These results applied to the [[algebraic fundamental group]] and to the [[Picard group]].

Another type of application are connectedness theorems such as [[Grothendieck's connectedness theorem]] (a local analogue of the [[Bertini theorem]]) or the [[Fulton–Hansen connectedness theorem]] due to {{harvtxt|Fulton|Hansen|1979}} and {{harvtxt|Faltings|1979}}. The latter asserts that for two [[projective variety|projective varieties]] ''V'' and ''W'' in '''P'''<sup>''r''</sup> over an [[algebraically closed field]], the [[connectedness dimension]] of ''Z'' = ''V'' ∩ ''W'' (i.e., the minimal dimension of a closed subset ''T'' of ''Z'' that has to be removed from ''Z'' so that the [[complement (set theory)|complement]] ''Z'' \ ''T'' is [[disconnected space|disconnected]]) is bound by
:c(''Z'') &ge; dim ''V'' + dim ''W'' &minus; ''r'' &minus; 1.
For example, ''Z'' is connected if dim ''V'' + dim ''W'' > ''r''.<ref>{{harvtxt|Brodmann|Sharp|1998|loc=§19.6}}</ref>

In polyhedral geometry, a key ingredient of Stanley's 1975 proof of the simplicial form of McMullen's [[Upper bound theorem]] involves showing that the [[Stanley-Reisner ring]] of the corresponding [[simplicial complex]] is [[Cohen-Macaulay]], and local cohomology is an important tool in this computation, via Hochster's formula.<ref>{{cite journal |title=How the Upper Bound Conjecture Was Proved|last=Stanley|first=Richard|year=2014|journal=[[Annals of Combinatorics]]|pages=533–539|volume=18|issue=3 |doi=10.1007/s00026-014-0238-5|s2cid=253585250 |hdl=1721.1/93189|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref name="stanley164"/><ref>{{harvtxt|Iyengar|Leuschke|Leykin|Miller|Miller|Singh|Walther|2007|loc=Lecture 16}}</ref>
